h-gui-lease:
## Parent notes

- run-4 final-clean critic analysis (line numbers are 9805d91; re-locate them in 346df29): Agent GUI-burst enforcement (stray kill plus gui_changes attribution) versus the human desktop session during a takeover. takeover closes the burst under gui_lock before it installs the lease (agentbox/service.py:503-521, close at 514) so that human changes stay out of agent bursts. But _snapshot (service.py:250-265) runs bursts.close('next_burst') and then bursts.open without gui_lock and without a lease check. decide calls it unconditionally (service.py:412), and the call_tool path checks the lease only in needs_snapshot (gui_bursts.py:58), before a multi-second commit. _run_tool then raises HumanControl (service.py:135-161), and the freshly opened burst stays installed through the lease with a baseline taken mid-takeover. close_idle (gui_bursts.py:137-148) treats a missing _gui_input_at as 0.0 and runs from every call_tool (service.py:271) and expire_stale. _stop_strays (gui_bursts.py:79-93) with gui_strays (gui_state.py) kills uid-1001 processes in sessions that are not in that baseline, which includes a terminal the human opened after it. _finish logs the human's /workspace edits as agent gui_changes.
- Since then: F2 fix makes _run_tool refuse GUI input without an open burst (GuiBursts.covers); F6 added AgentBox._lifecycle; N4 added the kept set (gui_bursts._kept) carried into the next baseline. Check whether these change the reachability of a burst opened during a lease, and what the kept set does when a burst spans a takeover.
- Runtime ordering with the real desktop is parent-live; propose an exact schedule (which call, which sleep, which observation) if you cannot settle it in the sandbox with fakes (tests/test_m2_unit.py has fakes for GuiBursts/AgentBox).

h-retention:
## Parent notes

- prune is host-CLI only and operates on the DB file directly; the attacker model is (a) an agent or network client influencing data that prune/verify later process (row contents, timestamps, approval statuses), (b) concurrent server writes during prune, (c) a person with DB write access but without the archive (documented limit: in-DB anchor is forgeable by DB writers; do not report that limit itself), and (d) operator mistakes the code claims to prevent (future cutoff, existing archive file, failure mid-way).
- tests/test_retention.py is Docker-free; run it in the sandbox. You can build SQLite fixtures in /scratch with agentbox.audit.AuditLog and call retention.prune on them.

h-lifecycle:
## Parent notes

- This unit came from the post-wave critic. Full critic boundary: Agent and human actions versus sandbox lifecycle state (F6 fix, PR #18). _lifecycle (service.py:500-505) is a per-sandbox mutex taken only by pause/resume/snapshot/restore/delete (service.py:507-540); call_tool, decide, import_file, takeover and the burst code never take it, so a tool exec, an approval decide or a pre-destructive snapshot can still run against a container that restore is replacing or delete is removing. Also: restore/snapshot hold the lock across a multi-second docker commit while log_human and end_desktop run inside it (human request threads and the Starlette threadpool can pile up behind one sandbox), self._life_locks (service.py:90) is a dict that grows per sandbox id and is never pruned, and SandboxManager.restore now refuses status 'deleted' (check that every other manager method that takes a snapshot, resume or exec has the same state guard). Invariant: after restore or delete returns, no agent or approved action writes to, snapshots, or records results for the old container or a deleted sandbox, no snapshot row or image is orphaned or attributed to the wrong container_id, and a lifecycle call cannot be starved or deadlocked by a tool call, takeover or burst close that holds _snap_locks, gui_lock or the per-sandbox concurrency slots.
- run-4 F6 (restore racing delete) is fixed by _lifecycle plus SandboxManager.restore refusing 'deleted'; look for the other pairs: call_tool/decide/_snapshot/import_file against restore/delete/pause. tests/test_m2_unit.py and test_m4_unit.py have fakes you can reuse in the sandbox. Real Docker timing is parent-live: give an exact schedule.

h-policy-cpu:
## Parent notes

- This unit came from the post-wave critic, based on h-approvals' measurement (Policy.decide 4.96 s for a 128 KiB 'x;' command). Full critic boundary: Agent to control-plane availability: pure-Python, CPU-bound policy and preview parsing of an attacker-sized command (up to the 8 MiB AGENTBOX_MAX_BODY; no per-command or per-argument length cap exists, grep finds only max_body_bytes) holds the GIL shared with the event loop and every human request thread. The h-approvals hunter measured Policy.decide at 4.96 s for a 128 KiB 'x;' command, growing at least linearly, and up to 4 such calls run concurrently per sandbox on the 32-thread tool_pool, across sandboxes. Invariant: no agent-supplied command or argument can make policy evaluation, _split_segments, simple_programs/shlex passes, _raw_hits or the preview glob/walk expansion cost more than a small bounded amount of CPU, memory or container-side exec time before the call is rejected or queued, and the human API stays responsive while it runs.
- Measure in the sandbox (bounded sizes only, e.g. 32/64/128/256 KiB) which function dominates and whether growth is linear or superlinear, and whether another thread (a stand-in for the event loop) is starved while it runs. Do not try full 8 MiB inputs in the 120 s sandbox; extrapolate. Check where in the call path a length cap would sit (before policy.decide) and what the agent token can reach.
